blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 27 (Biochemistry), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 What are carbohydrates? Describe monosaccharides: their general formula, classification by number of carbon atoms and by functional group, and their open-chain and ring forms. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Carbohydrates: naturally occurring organic compounds (sugars, starch, cellulose, substances of bacterial cell walls and insect exoskeletons), major sources of energy in our diet. Chemically they are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or their derived compounds.

Monosaccharides: the simplest carbohydrates (sugars); they cannot be hydrolysed into simpler compounds. General formula Cₙ(H₂O)y, n = 3 to 7. Examples: glucose and fructose.

By number of carbon atoms: 3 C triose, 4 C tetrose, 5 C pentose, 6 C hexose, etc.
By functional group: an aldose contains an aldehydic group (glucose); a ketose contains a ketonic group (fructose).

Open-chain and ring forms: monosaccharides exist as open chains or rings, and the two forms are interconvertible. Pentoses and hexoses are more stable and more abundant as rings. Fructose forms a five-membered ring (furanose); glucose forms a six-membered ring (pyranose). In solution too most molecules are rings, in equilibrium with a very small amount of the open-chain form.

book_ref.quote: Chemically, they are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or their derived compounds.

blocks.prompt: 2 Explain how hydrogen bonding accounts for the physical properties of monosaccharides. Why is honey thick? Name the natural sources of glucose and fructose. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Sugar molecules have many hydroxyl (–OH) groups.

Solid state: the –OH groups form extensive hydrogen bonding between sugar molecules, so pure monosaccharides are solids.
Solubility: in solution they form extensive hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so they are highly soluble in water.
Honey: glucose and fructose are present in honey in high concentration; their strong and intensive hydrogen bonding gives honey its thickness and viscosity.

Sources and use: glucose is called blood sugar because it is present in human blood; fructose is abundant in fruits and honey. Monosaccharides are an excellent source of instant energy in living organisms.

book_ref.quote: The presence of many hydroxyl groups (–OH) in the sugar molecules

blocks.prompt: 3 What are disaccharides? Explain their formation by a condensation reaction with an equation, and describe the glycosidic bond using sucrose as an example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Disaccharides: carbohydrates of two monosaccharide units joined by a glycosidic linkage, general formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Common examples: sucrose, lactose and maltose.

Formation (condensation): the hydroxyl group of one monosaccharide combines with a hydrogen of another monosaccharide through a covalent bond, and a molecule of water is released:
C₆H₁₂O₆ + C₆H₁₂O₆ → C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O

Glycosidic bond: the C–O–C bond that links the two units is called the glycosidic bond.

Example: sucrose, the common table sugar, is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose joined by a glycosidic bond:
glucose + fructose → sucrose + water

book_ref.quote: The bond C–O–C is known as the glycosidic bond.

blocks.prompt: 4 Why is cellulose called a structural polysaccharide while starch and glycogen are storage polysaccharides? Explain with reference to their structures and where they are found. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
All three are polysaccharides of glucose units, general formula (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ.

Storage polysaccharides:
• Starch is the main energy store of plants (potato, sugar beet, rice, grains). It has two components: amylose (long, unbranched chains with many glycosidic linkages) and amylopectin (a compact, highly branched structure).
• Glycogen (animal starch) is a glucose polymer stored in the liver and muscles of animals. Its structure is very similar to amylopectin but more highly branched. Excess glucose is stored as glycogen.

Structural polysaccharide:
• Cellulose is the major structural material of plant cell walls and makes most of the leaves, branches and trunk. Its glucose units form long unbranched chains linked by glycosidic bonds; these chains form strong hydrogen bonds with each other, making cellulose rigid and insoluble in water. In human food it serves as fibre, which improves gut health.

book_ref.quote: Starch is the main storage of energy in plants

blocks.prompt: 5 A sample of starch, (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ, has molar mass 81 000 g mol⁻¹. (i) Find n. (ii) On complete hydrolysis each C₆H₁₀O₅ unit takes up one H₂O and gives one glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆. What mass of glucose is obtained from 81 g of this starch? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Divide the molar mass by the mass of one unit; then each mole of units gives one mole of glucose.

book_ref.quote: Polysaccharides give simple sugars, i.e., monosaccharides on hydrolysis.

steps: Mass of one unit C₆H₁₀O₅ = 6(12) + 10(1) + 5(16) = 162 g mol⁻¹
(ii) Moles of units in 81 g = 81 ÷ 162 = 0.50 mol, so glucose formed = 0.50 mol
Molar mass of C₆H₁₂O₆ = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180 g mol⁻¹; mass of glucose = 0.50 × 180 = 90 g

blocks.prompt: 6 Describe the nutritional importance of carbohydrates and the risks of imbalance in their intake. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Carbohydrates are essential for energy and nutrient intake; the type and amount consumed strongly affect health.

Glucose (simple sugars):
• Primary source of energy for cells; easily absorbed and metabolised, 1 g of glucose gives about 15.6 kJ.
• Excess glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles.
• Normal blood glucose is 70-110 mg/dL, controlled by the hormones insulin and glucagon.
• Above the normal range it can lead to diabetes, a chronic condition when the pancreas does not produce enough insulin or the body cannot use it effectively. Uncontrolled diabetes causes hyperglycemia (high blood sugar), which over time damages nerves and blood vessels.
• Insufficient carbohydrate causes fatigue and reduced physical and mental performance.

Fructose and refined sugars: fructose provides energy, but high intake causes obesity. Diets high in refined sugars are linked with diabetes, heart disease and certain cancers; complex carbohydrates and fibres are protective.

Sparing of proteins and fats: with sufficient carbohydrates the body uses them for energy instead of breaking down proteins or fats.

book_ref.quote: Carbohydrates have a complex role in the human health.

blocks.prompt: 7 A person has a blood glucose level of 95 mg/dL and a blood volume of 5.0 dm³ (1 dm³ = 10 dL). (i) Is this level within the normal range? (ii) Calculate the mass of glucose in the blood. (iii) How much energy would this glucose provide, if 1 g gives about 15.6 kJ? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Compare with 70-110 mg/dL, convert the blood volume to dL, multiply by the concentration, then use 15.6 kJ per gram.

book_ref.quote: with 1 g of glucose providing about 15.6 kJ

steps: (i) Normal range is 70-110 mg/dL; 95 mg/dL lies within it
(ii) Blood volume = 5.0 dm³ × 10 dL dm⁻³ = 50 dL
Mass of glucose = 95 mg dL⁻¹ × 50 dL = 4750 mg = 4.75 g
blocks.final_answer: (i) Yes, normal; (ii) 4.75 g of glucose; (iii) about 74 kJ (74.1 kJ)

blocks.prompt: 8 Explain the formation of a peptide bond and a polypeptide chain. Describe the primary structure of a protein and show, with the example of sickle cell anemia, why the amino acid sequence matters. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Proteins are linear chains of amino acids (about 20 kinds) linked by peptide bonds.

Peptide bond: an amide bond formed when the –COO⁻ group of one amino acid reacts with the –NH₃⁺ group of the adjacent amino acid; repeated, this gives a linear polymer.
Polypeptide chain: the long chain of amino acids formed by many peptide linkages. Each protein has specific polypeptide chains which determine its structure and function.

Primary structure: the specific linear sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds in a polypeptide chain. This sequence decides how the protein folds into its three-dimensional shape, which defines its biological function. Albumin and insulin depend on their precise sequences.

Importance of sequence: even a small change in a single amino acid can alter the structure and impair function. In sickle cell anemia, abnormal formation of haemoglobin deforms normal red blood cells into sickle-shaped cells; these clog the blood veins and disrupt normal circulation.

book_ref.quote: Proteins are linear chains of amino acids that are linked together by peptide bonds.

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe the secondary structure of proteins. Compare the α-helix with the β-pleated sheet and state the importance of these arrangements. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Secondary structure arises when the backbone atoms form hydrogen bonds within a polypeptide chain, producing regular patterns: α-helices and β-pleated sheets. These arrangements give stability and flexibility and contribute to the overall three-dimensional shape that the protein's biological function needs.

book_ref.quote: The secondary structure of a protein arises when the backbone atoms form hydrogen bonds

rows: Hydrogen bonds form along a single chain
Hydrogen bonds form between adjacent polypeptide strands
Coiled, spiral structure
Folded, sheet-like structure
Example: keratin
Example: silk fibroin

blocks.prompt: 10 Classify proteins on the basis of their overall shape. Describe fibrous and globular proteins with examples, and explain denaturing of proteins. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
After tertiary or quaternary structure formation, proteins are divided by overall shape into two main classes.

Denaturing: globular proteins are sensitive to heat and pH. Egg white hardens on heating because the hydrogen bonding between the chains is disrupted and the chains open up; milk protein casein coagulates when the pH is changed by adding lemon juice. This is called denaturing of proteins.

book_ref.quote: These proteins consist of long, rod-like, or thread-like molecules

rows: Long, rod-like or thread-like molecules
Whole molecule spherical or ovoid
Chains run parallel, linked by strong hydrogen bonds or disulphide bonds into fibres
Chains folded into a compact shape
Generally insoluble, mechanically strong and stable
More sensitive to heat and pH
Structural polymers: collagen, keratin, myosin
Worker proteins: enzymes, hormones, nutrients; egg white

blocks.prompt: 11 Describe the biological functions of proteins, giving an example of each kind. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Proteins are grouped by their biological and metabolic functions:

• Hormonal proteins: regulate physiological activities such as growth, development, metabolism and reproduction; e.g. insulin from the pancreas regulates movement of glucose from blood into cells.
• Storage proteins: provide nutrients for germinating seedlings or early development of animals; e.g. ferritin stores iron.
• Structural proteins: the most abundant in a vertebrate body; fibrous, give shape and support; e.g. keratin in hair, fibrin in blood clots, collagen; they form the matrix of skin, ligaments, tendons and bones.
• Contractile proteins: actin and myosin make the thin and thick filaments of muscle for contraction and relaxation.
• Defensive proteins: fight infection; e.g. antibodies bind specific antigens and destroy them.
• Transport (carrier) proteins: move molecules and ions across membranes; e.g. haemoglobin carries oxygen between lungs and tissues.
• Receptor proteins: in the cell membrane; receive chemical signals.
• Regulatory proteins: control cellular and physiological activities; e.g. insulin regulates sugar metabolism; growth hormone.

book_ref.quote: Proteins can be grouped into different categories based on their biological and metabolic functions.

blocks.prompt: 12 What are enzymes? Explain the role of the active site in enzyme specificity and describe the lock and key model. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts for chemical reactions in living organisms. They speed up a reaction to an extent impossible without them; e.g. one molecule of carbonic anhydrase converts about a million CO₂ and H₂O molecules to carbonic acid in one second.

Active site: a special site on the enzyme surface which binds the substrate and converts it into products.

Specificity: each enzyme acts on one particular substrate because its active site has a unique shape that only that substrate fits. Random movement brings the substrate into the active site, forming a temporary enzyme–substrate complex; the products are then released and the enzyme remains unchanged, free to bind another substrate:
E + S → ES complex → E + products

Lock and key model (Emil Fischer, 1894): the enzyme is the lock, the substrate is the key and the active site is the keyhole. Only the correctly shaped key (substrate) fits into the keyhole of the lock.

book_ref.quote: An enzyme has a special site on its surface, called the active site

blocks.prompt: 13 One molecule of carbonic anhydrase converts about 10⁶ molecules of CO₂ (with water) to carbonic acid per second. (i) How many CO₂ molecules does one enzyme molecule convert in one hour? (ii) How many enzyme molecules are needed to convert 1.8 × 10¹⁰ CO₂ molecules in one second? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Multiply the turnover by the time in seconds; for (ii) divide the molecules to be converted by the turnover of one enzyme.

book_ref.quote: turnover about 10⁶ per second

steps: (ii) One enzyme molecule converts 10⁶ molecules in one second

blocks.prompt: 14 Describe the factors that affect the activity of enzymes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The important factors are temperature, pH and the concentrations of substrate and enzyme; enzyme action is also affected by substances such as co-enzymes, activators and inhibitors.

Temperature and pH: the temperature and pH that give maximum activity are the optimum temperature and optimum pH. If they are disturbed from the optimum values the enzyme action can be deactivated. Enzymatic reactions in the human body and other organisms occur best at or around 37 °C.

Concentration of enzyme and substrate: the rate increases as the enzyme or substrate concentration is increased, because more molecules provide more binding sites and more enzyme-substrate complex forms.

Other substances: co-enzymes and activators assist enzyme action, while inhibitors cause the enzyme to lose its activity.

book_ref.quote: The enzyme action may also be affected in the presence of some other substances

blocks.prompt: 15 What are enzyme inhibitors? Explain reversible (competitive) inhibition with the example of malonate, and irreversible inhibition with the example of penicillin. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Inhibitors are small molecules or ions that make enzymes lose their catalytic activity; all of them prevent the active site from binding the substrate.

Reversible (competitive) inhibitors: molecules with the same shape as the substrate; substrate and inhibitor compete for the active site, and the inhibitor is held by non-covalent bonds. The more the inhibitor, the more the enzyme is deactivated for its substrate.
Example: succinate dehydrogenase oxidises butanedioate (succinate ion), ⁻OOC–CH₂–CH₂–COO⁻. Propanedioate (malonate), ⁻OOC–CH₂–COO⁻, resembles it and inhibits the enzyme.

Irreversible inhibitors: small ions or molecules that bind to the enzyme permanently, often by covalent bonds, so the enzyme loses activity permanently. (They are not the same as non-competitive inhibitors, which bind elsewhere on the enzyme, change the shape of the active site and usually bind reversibly.) Such inhibition can cause severe health issues or death. Poisons, antibiotics, anti-metabolites and some drugs act this way.
Example: penicillin blocks the enzyme trans-peptidase, which synthesises the bacterial cell wall, and so kills bacteria.

book_ref.quote: A variety of small molecules or ions that cause enzymes to lose their catalytic activity are called inhibitors.

blocks.prompt: 16 What are simple lipids? Describe triglycerides (fats and oils) and waxes, with their properties and uses. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Simple lipids are esters of fatty acids with different alcohols; they are sub-classified as fats, oils and waxes.

Triglycerides: animal fats and vegetable oils are esters of one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids (which may be similar or different):
glycerol + 3 fatty acids → triglyceride + 3 H₂O
• Fats contain saturated fatty acids and are solid at room temperature; oils contain unsaturated fatty acids with one or more double bonds.
• Efficient energy-storage molecules; also give insulation, protect organs and are a source of fat-soluble vitamins.
• Hydrophobic fatty acid chains make fats insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents, so they form insulating layers under the skin and cushioning around organs such as the kidneys.

Waxes: long fatty-acid chains esterified to long-chain alcohols; both chains are nonpolar and hydrophobic. They form protective coatings that prevent water from sticking to surfaces, e.g. beeswax (main ester myricyl palmitate, CH₃(CH₂)₁₄COO(CH₂)₂₉CH₃), the oil in a whale's head, feathers of some aquatic birds, plant waxes. Used in lotions, ointments and polishes.

book_ref.quote: Simple lipids are sub-classified based on the type of alcohols

blocks.prompt: 17 What are compound lipids? Describe the structure of phospholipids and the formation of a bilayer, and give the roles of lipoproteins, glycolipids and liposomes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Compound lipids are esters of fatty acids with alcohols containing an additional group such as phosphate, a nitrogenous base, carbohydrate or protein.

Phospholipids: like a fat but only two fatty acids are attached to glycerol; the third –OH of glycerol is linked to a phosphate group, which makes the molecule polar. The hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic, while the phosphate group and its attached components form a hydrophilic head.

Bilayer: in water, phospholipids form a double-layered sheet (bilayer): the polar heads face outward and the non-polar tails cluster together in their own layer. This forms the structure of all cell membranes.

Lipoproteins: complexes of lipids and proteins that transport hydrophobic lipids (cholesterol and triglycerides) in the bloodstream.
Glycolipids: lipids with carbohydrate groups attached, mostly in nervous tissue.
Liposomes: artificial phospholipid structures, a lipid bilayer around a watery core; they encapsulate water-soluble (e.g. cancer) drugs, shield them from degradation, improve solubility and give targeted delivery to tumour cells.

book_ref.quote: The hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic

blocks.prompt: 18 What are derived lipids? Describe terpenes and carotenoids, and explain why steroids are grouped with lipids, naming the steroids found in living systems. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Derived (associated) lipids: hydrolytic products of simple and compound lipids that have lipid characteristics, e.g. fatty acids, glycerol, steroids and lipid-soluble vitamins. They are not fats themselves but come from fats, and they play roles in energy and hormone production, cell structure, nerve health and vitamin function.

Terpenes: a wide variety of plant hydrocarbons (essential oils) built from isoprene units, CH₂=C(CH₃)–CH=CH₂ (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene, C₅H₈). Terpenes containing 40 carbon atoms are carotenoids. Limonene is an example of a terpene.

Steroids: not formed from fatty acids but have some lipid-like properties, so they are grouped with lipids. The steroid nucleus is three cyclohexane rings and one cyclopentane ring fused together, named A, B, C and D. Many steroids also carry an –OH group, which places them in the alcohol class (sterols).
Steroids in biological systems: cholesterol, bile salts, vitamin D and steroid hormones.

book_ref.quote: They perform important roles in the body including energy and hormone production

blocks.prompt: 19 Describe the nutritional and biological importance of lipids. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
• Energy storage: a major function of lipids is to be the primary energy store of living organisms. On oxidation to carbon dioxide and water they have a higher caloric value, so they give more energy per gram than carbohydrates.
• Fat-soluble vitamins: lipids act as solvents for the transport of vitamins A, D, E and K and help their absorption into intestinal cells and then the bloodstream; these vitamins should be eaten with a bit of healthy fat.
• Insulation: because of their non-polar nature fats insulate the body from water, heat and electricity; they also form layers under the skin and cushion organs.
• Hibernation: animals such as polar bears, reptiles and amphibians store extra fat when hibernating; fat is a more concentrated energy source than glycogen, so stored fat is used effectively while metabolic rate is very low.
• Other roles (27.4): fuel molecules, signal molecules, membrane components, hormones and intracellular messengers.

book_ref.quote: Lipids act as solvents for the transport of fat vitamins

blocks.prompt: 20 What are nucleic acids? Describe how nucleotides join to form a polynucleotide chain, naming the sugars present and the linkage involved. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Nucleic acids are large biomolecules that store and transmit genetic information; they are polymers of smaller units called nucleotides.

Structure: a nucleic acid is a nucleotide chain of alternating sugar and phosphate groups, with organic (nitrogenous) bases attached to the sugar molecules.
Sugars: ribose in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA; both are five-carbon sugars.

Linkage: nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester linkages through the 5' and 3' carbon atoms of the sugar; the 3' O–P bond is single and P=O is on a non-bridging oxygen. Repeated up to several million times, this gives a polynucleotide.
…–sugar(3')–O–P(=O)(O⁻)–O–(5')sugar–…

Strength: phosphodiester linkages are strong covalent bonds, giving strength and stability to the polynucleotide chain.

book_ref.quote: Nucleic acids are formed from the nucleotide chains

blocks.prompt: 21 Describe the double helix structure of DNA proposed by Watson and Crick, including base pairing, and explain the importance of replication. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick showed that DNA consists of two polynucleotide chains.

• Each chain forms a right-handed helical spiral, and the two chains coil around each other to form a double helix.
• The chains are not identical but opposite to each other due to base pairing: the 3' end of one faces the 5' end of the other.
• Each chain has a sugar-phosphate backbone; the bases project at right angles and are held by weak hydrogen bonds to the bases of the opposite chain.
• Base pairing: adenine (A) is always opposite thymine (T) with two hydrogen bonds; guanine (G) is opposite cytosine (C) with three hydrogen bonds.
• The sequence of the four bases stores the genetic information, which is transmitted efficiently and accurately for protein synthesis.

Replication: the process during the cell cycle in which DNA is copied, so that on cell division each new cell receives a complete set of genetic material. In this way genetic information passes to daughter cells and to the next generation.

book_ref.quote: Each chain has a sugar-phosphate backbone

blocks.prompt: 22 Answer the following about DNA base pairing. (i) One strand of a DNA segment reads A-T-G-G-C-A-T-C-G-C. Write the complementary strand and find the total number of hydrogen bonds between the two strands. (ii) A DNA segment has 30 base pairs, of which 12 are G–C pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold its strands together? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Pair A with T and G with C; count A–T pairs × 2 and G–C pairs × 3.

book_ref.quote: There are two hydrogen bonds between A and T pair

steps: A–T pairs (A, T, A, T) = 4 → 4 × 2 = 8; G–C pairs (G, G, C, C, G, C) = 6 → 6 × 3 = 18; total = 26

blocks.prompt: 23 Compare the structure of DNA and RNA. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Both are nucleic acids: polynucleotide chains of sugar and phosphate groups with nitrogenous bases, joined by phosphodiester linkages. They differ as follows:

book_ref.quote: RNA is usually single stranded unlike DNA

rows: Two polynucleotide chains coiled into a right-handed double helix
Usually single stranded; the chain can fold back on itself into a helical loop
Sugar: deoxyribose
Sugar: ribose
Bases A, T, G, C (A–T and G–C paired by hydrogen bonds)
Bases A, U, G, C
Present in the nucleus; carries the genetic instructions and copies itself by replication
Three major types: mRNA, rRNA, tRNA, which work in protein synthesis

blocks.prompt: 24 What is a gene? Explain how the instructions of a gene are converted into a protein molecule, stating where each step takes place. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Gene: a specific region (section) of DNA that carries genetic information and provides the instructions for the cell to make a particular protein.

Protein synthesis needs two processes, transcription and translation.

Transcription (in the nucleus): the genetic instructions for making a protein are copied from a DNA gene into messenger RNA (mRNA). When the mRNA strand is complete, it detaches from DNA and enters the cytoplasm.

Translation (at the ribosomes in the cytoplasm): mRNA attaches to ribosomes (made with the help of rRNA). The code carried by mRNA is read and converted into a specific sequence of amino acids; tRNA translates the mRNA nucleotide sequence into the corresponding amino acids. The tRNA molecules release their amino acids, which join into a polypeptide chain; the chain grows as bonds form between amino acids until the complete protein is formed.

DNA gene → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation at ribosome) → protein

book_ref.quote: Two processes, transcription and translation are required

blocks.prompt: 25 What are minerals? Classify them into macro- and micro-minerals with examples, and describe the roles of calcium, phosphorus and zinc in nutrition. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Minerals are inorganic substances necessary for certain physiochemical life processes. They produce no energy, but have important functions in various activities.

Classification:
• Macro (major) minerals, needed in amounts greater than about 100 mg per day: calcium, phosphorus, sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium and sulfur.
• Micro (trace) minerals, needed in amounts less than about 100 mg per day: iron, copper, cobalt, iodine, zinc, manganese, molybdenum, fluoride, chromium and selenium.

Roles (Table 27.1):
• Calcium (milk and dairy, greens, broccoli, salmon, sardines, beans): formation of bones and teeth, normal blood clotting, muscle contraction and relaxation, heart and nerve function.
• Phosphorus (meat, fish, poultry, eggs, milk, cereals): formation of bones and teeth; regulates the release and use of body energy (ATP); carries fat as part of phospholipids; maintains normal acid/base balance.
• Zinc (meat, seafood, whole grains): component of many enzyme systems (growth, immune function); found in the hormone insulin.

book_ref.quote: Minerals are inorganic substances, necessary for the maintenance of certain physiochemical life processes
